never allow myself to feel or express anger
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette: Kaito had always been driven by a desire to tell the stories that needed to be told. As a young journalist, he had a knack for getting to the heart of a story and conveying it in a way that resonated with his readers. But one fateful night, Kaito's own story took a devastating turn. He was walking home from a late-night shift at the newsroom when his boyfriend, Alex, confronted him on the street. The argument escalated quickly, and before Kaito knew it, he was being pushed to the ground and punched repeatedly. The memory of that night still feels like it's happening in real-time for Kaito. He can recall the sound of Alex's labored breathing, the feeling of his fist connecting with Kaito's cheekbone, and the searing pain that shot through his body as he fell to the ground. When the memory returns, Kaito is overwhelmed by emotion, his mind racing with thoughts of "what if" and "why me." He often has to stop whatever he's doing and take a few moments to collect himself. In the months following the attack, Kaito began to notice changes in his behavior. He started taking buses less frequently, opting instead to walk or ride his bike whenever possible. The thought of being alone on a bus with strangers made him anxious, especially if there were men nearby. He found himself constantly scanning his surroundings, searching for potential threats. Kaito's relationship with Alex had been tumultuous from the start, but he couldn't shake the feeling that he was somehow to blame for what happened. He began dwelling on all the things he could have done differently – ways he might have avoided triggering Alex's anger or placated him more effectively. These ruminations consumed Kaito, making it difficult for him to focus on his work or enjoy time with friends. As a journalist, Kaito was used to being assertive and direct, but since the attack, he had become increasingly passive, never allowing himself to express anger or frustration, even when provoked. He started to restrict his eating habits as well, using food avoidance as a way of coping with stress and anxiety. His partner, Rachel, noticed the changes in Kaito's behavior and encouraged him to seek help. Kaito's difficulty sleeping was another issue that had been plaguing him. He would wake up multiple times throughout the night, checking his locks, windows, and doors to ensure they were secure. Even when Rachel reassured him that everything was fine, he couldn't shake off the feeling of unease. Delays or unexpected events – like a traffic jam or a missed phone call – sent Kaito's mind racing with worst-case scenarios. When asked about his fears, Kaito's response is simple: "You can never know who will harm you." He looks around at the world and sees potential threats lurking in every corner. People, he believes, are inherently untrustworthy. This mistrust has seeped into all areas of his life, making it difficult for him to form close relationships or trust his own instincts. Kaito's sense of inadequacy is another lingering concern. He often wonders if he's somehow flawed or weak, that there must be something fundamentally wrong with him for Alex to have treated him the way he did. This self-doubt has begun to erode Kaito's confidence as a journalist and as a person. Rachel's support and encouragement finally convinced Kaito to seek professional help. He hopes that therapy will provide him with tools to manage his symptoms, work through his negative appraisals, and rebuild his sense of trust in himself and others. What he fears most is that he'll never be able to shake off the memories of that fateful night or regain a sense of safety and security.
